title: 000 Introduction
text:
000 Introduction

(*

Semity Proof Assistant

Theodoric E Stier
theodoric.stier@gmail.com
October 2025
 
# Introduction

The purpose of this proof assistant is to
demonstrate the mechanics of formal proof.
It is based on a semi-typed lambda calculus.
A lambda calculus is a system for computing.
Semi-typed means that terms are judged for
validity and judgment might not terminate.

The types of this lambda calculus are called
propositions, and the terms are called proofs.
There are a few top-level directives which
introduce propositions and proofs.

The first line of a chapter is interpreted
as the name of the chapter. The table of
contents sorts chapters alphabetically by
name.

Rulers:            20                  40

*)

title: 010 Propositions
text:
010 Propositions

(*

# Propositions

Propositions are types that correspond to
sentences in higher order logic.

A proposition name is any nonempty sequence
of word or digit characters such as `true`
or `42`.

## Kinds of Propositions

There are four kinds of propositions:

- A proposition can be a proposition name.
Such a proposition as `true` is called a
reference proposition.

- A proposition can be constructed from two
others by inserting an arrow between them.
Such a proposition as `true -> false` is
called an arrow proposition.

- A proposition can be constructed from two
others by juxtaposition. Such a proposition
as `not false` is called an application proposition.

- A proposition can be constructed from another
by prepending a binding clause. Such a proposition
as `\x.subset x empty_set` is called a lambda
proposition.

## Proposition Syntax Rules

Binding clauses with multiple binders such
as in `\a b.a` are short hand for nested
lambdas such as `\a.\b.a`. Binding clauses
with no binders such as `\.` are allowed.

Parentheses are required in various places.
Binding clauses have last precedence. Arrows
have second to last precedence and associate
to the right. Juxtapositions have highest
precedence and associate to the left. 

`\a.b c` = `\a.(b c)`
`a \b.c` = `a (\b.c)`
`\a.b -> c` = `\a.(b -> c)`
`a -> \b.c` = `a -> (\b.c)`
`a -> b c` = `a -> (b c)`
`a b -> c` = `(a b) -> c`
`a -> b -> c` = `a -> (b -> c)`
`a b c` = `(a b) c`

## `define` Directive

Proposition names may be defined globally
and in any proof. The `define` directive
names a proposition that is defined. Write
its name, then `:=`, then a proposition which
defines it, then `.`.

*)

-- Identity
define id :=
\a.a.

-- Left of Two
define const :=
\a b.a.

-- Right of Two
define seq :=
\a b.b.

-- Unary Tuple
define di :=
\a f.f a.

-- Binary Tuple
define pair :=
\a b f.f a b.

-- Composition
define comp :=
\f g x.f (g x).

-- Binary Permutation
define flip :=
\f a b.f b a.

-- Arrow
define ar :=
\a b.a -> b.

-- Reverse Arrow
define rar :=
\a b.b -> a.

-- Binary Arrow
define bar :=
\a b c.a -> b -> c.

(*

## Proposition Semantic Rules

Propositions must be closed, meaning no variable
occurs free. Here, the proposition `foo`
causes an error because `foo` is free in
the context.

*)

-- define x := foo.

(*

Propositions also compute when a lambda expands
on the left side of an application. The `print`
directive queries a proposition and prints it.
Write the proposition, then `.`.

*)

-- print cons a b car.

title: 011 Proofs
text:
011 Proofs (* # Proofs Proofs are terms that correspond to natural deduction. A proof name such as `` begins with `<` and ends with `>`. Those can contain any nonempty sequence of word, digit, or non-newline whitespace characters. ## Kinds of Proofs There are seven kinds of proofs: - A proof can be a proof name. Such a proof as `` is called a reference proof. - A proof can be constructed from two others by juxtaposition. Such a proof as ` ` is called a modus ponens proof. - A proof can be constructed from a proof and a proposition by juxtaposition. Such a proof as ` false` is called a specialization proof. - A proof can be constructed from another by prepending an introduction binding clause. Such a proof as `given x. x y` is called an introduction proof. - A proof can be constructed from another by prepending a conditional proof binding clause. Such a proof as `premise : y.` is called a conditional proof. - A proof can be constructed from another by prepending an definition clause. Such a proof as `let x := pair a b.pair x x` is called a definition proof. - A proof can be constructed from another by prepending a lemma clause. Such a proof as `lemma := a b.<> ` is called a lemma proof. ## Proof Syntax Rules Introduction binding clauses with multiple binders such as in `given a b.` are short hand for nested introductions such as `given a.given b.`. Binding clauses with no binders such as `given.` are allowed. A conditional proof or lemma proof may omit the `:` and proposition. Brackets are required in various places. Juxtapositions have highest precedence and associate to the left. Binding clauses have last precedence. `given a.b c` = `given a.[b c]` `a given b.c` = `a [given b.c]` `premise . c` = `premise .[ c]` ` premise .` = ` [premise .]` `a b c` = `[a b] c` ## Proof Semantic Rules Proofs are judged according to validation rules. When proofs are judged, judgment might not terminate. When judgment terminates, the proofs correspond to formal proofs of corresponding statements of their propositions. Judgment attempts to infer the proposition of a conditional proof or lemma proof that omits its `:` and proposition. ## `theorem` directive The `theorem` directive names a proof and a proposition that it shows. Write its name, then `:`, then the proposition shown, then `:=`, then a proof which shows the proposition, then `.`. *) theorem : \a.a -> a := -- For all `a`, `a` implies `a`." given a. premise : a. . (* While writing the proof, the output window displays messages and goals. Each goal is printed along with its context. For example, when we have this partial proof of `` given a. premise : a. . the output window will display the goal a : a ⊢ a The proof steps proceed by introducing proposition `a` and premise `` showing `a`. `a` and `` are listed in the context of the enclosed goal. The last step references `` to show the goal. When all proofs are okay, the output window will display "👍" to indicate the approval of the sacred boar at the center of the world. Introduction proofs break down lambda goals by binding proposition names. A proposition name bound by an introduction proof is called a variable. Conditional proofs break down arrow goals by binding proof names. A proof name bound by a conditional proof is called a premise. *) define left := \a b.a -> b -> a. define right := \a b.a -> b -> b. theorem : left := -- For all `a` and `b`... given a b. premise : a. premise : b. . theorem : right := given a b. premise : a. b. (* Here, ` b` is specialized for `b`. E.g. Say we have the following context and goal. a ⊢ \b.a -> b -> b The introduction clause `given z.` adds variable `z` to the context and specializes the goal. a z ⊢ a -> z -> z The conditional proof clause `premise : a.` adds premise `` (which shows `a`) to the context and removes the antecedent from the goal. a z ha : a ⊢ z -> z Here are a few basic proofs that we will use many times. *) theorem : \a b.a -> (a -> b) -> b := given a b. premise : a. premise : a -> b. . theorem : \a b c.a -> b -> (a -> b -> c) -> c := given a b c. premise : a. premise : b. premise : a -> b -> c. . theorem : \a b c.(a -> b -> c) -> b -> a -> c := given a b c. premise : a -> b -> c. premise : b. premise : a. . theorem : \a b c.(a -> b) -> (b -> c) -> a -> c := given a b c. premise : a -> b. premise : b -> c. premise : a. [ ]. theorem : \a b c.(b -> c) -> (a -> b) -> a -> c := given a b c. \. a b c. theorem : \a b.(a -> a -> b) -> a -> b := given a b. premise : a -> a -> b. premise : a. . theorem : \p x.p -> p x := given p x. premise

: p.

x. theorem : \x p q.x q -> (\x.x q -> x p) -> x p := given x p q. premise : x q. premise

: \x.x q -> x p.

x .

title: 020 Truth
text:
020 Truth (* # Truth Barendregt neatly defines the typical logical connectives in terms of universal quantification and implication. We follow this approach and benefit from its generality. `false` and `not` are defined so that `false` is negated and negations imply `false`. `true` is defined as the negation of false. truth is the first truth condition. `not` is the second truth condition. There is a third truth conditionintroduced later, called `irrefutable`, which refers to a negation of a negation. `true` is the negation of false, and `false` is the negation of `true`, so there are only two truth values. *) define false := \a.a. define not := \a.a -> false. define true := not false. theorem : true := false. theorem : not true -> false := true false . theorem : \a.false -> a := given a. premise : false. a. theorem : \a x.a -> (not a) -> x := given a x. premise : a. premise : not a. x. theorem : \a x.not a -> a -> x := given a x. premise : not a. premise : a. x. theorem : \p x.not (p x) -> not p := given p x. premise : not (p x). premise

: p. \.

x.

title: 021 Relations
text:
021 Relations

(*

These are the elementary properties of relations.
These properties will be proven for relations
such as conjunction or equality.

*)

-- Reflexivity
define reflexive :=
\f a.f a a.

-- Symmetry
define symmetric :=
\f a b.f a b -> f b a.

-- Transitivity
define transitive :=
\f a b c.f a b -> f b c -> f a c.

-- Transitivity (Reverse)
define transitive_reverse :=
\f a b c.f b c -> f a b -> f a c.

title: 031 Contradiction
text:
031 Contradiction

(*

Irrefutability is negation of negation.
It's the third truth condition.

Definite things are true when they are irrefutable.
Triple negation collapse is the fact that
negations are regular.

*)

define irrefutable :=
\a.not (not a).

define regular :=
\x.irrefutable x -> x.

theorem <irrefutable of> :
\a.a -> irrefutable a :=

given a.
<syllogy> a false
.

theorem <negative converse> :
\a b.(a -> b) -> not b -> not a :=

given a b.
<implication transitive> a b false.

theorem <symmetric converse> :
\a b.(a -> not b) -> b -> not a :=

given a b.
<implication reverse> a b false.

theorem <irrefutable converse> :
\a b.(not a -> not b) -> b -> irrefutable a :=

given a b.
<implication reverse> (not a) b false.

theorem <regular converse> :
\a b.regular a -> (not a -> not b) -> b -> a :=

given a b.
premise <r> : regular a.
premise <n> : not a -> not b.
<implication transitive reverse> <r> \.
<irrefutable converse> <n>.
 
theorem <negation regular> :
\a.regular (not a) :=

given a.
<negative converse> \.
<irrefutable of>.

theorem <negated implication> :
\a b.not (a -> b) -> not b :=

given a b.
<negative converse> \.
<left>.

theorem <negative contradiction> :
\a.(a -> not a) -> not a :=

given a.
<trivial implication>.

theorem <irrefutable contradiction> :
\a.(not a -> a) -> irrefutable a :=

given a.
premise <hf> : not a -> a.
<trivial implication> \.
<implication transitive> \.
<hf>.

theorem <regular contradiction> :
\a.regular a -> (not a -> a) -> a :=

given a.
premise <hd> : regular a.
premise <hf> : not a -> a.
<hd> \.
<irrefutable contradiction> \.
<hf>.

theorem <irrefutable implication> :
\a b.(a -> b) -> irrefutable a -> irrefutable b :=

given a b.
premise <hab> : a -> b.
premise <hia> : irrefutable a.
premise <hnb> : not b.
<hia> \.
<negative converse> <hab> \.
<hnb>.

title: 032 Junction
text:
032 Junction

(*

These are the logical junctions as defined
by Barendregt et al.

*)

define and :=
\a b c.(a -> b -> c) -> c.

define or :=
\a b c.(a -> c) -> (b -> c) -> c.

define either :=
\a b.not (and (not a) (not b)).

define iff :=
\a b.and (a -> b) (b -> a).

theorem <conjunction introduction> :
\a b.a -> b -> and a b :=

given a b.
premise <a>.
premise <b>.
given c.
<binary syllogy> <a> <b>.
 
theorem <reverse conjunction introduction> :
\a b.b -> a -> and a b :=

given a b.
<implication reverse> \.
<conjunction introduction>.
 
theorem <conjunction elimination> :
\a b c.(a -> b -> c) -> and a b -> c :=

given a b c.
premise <habc> : a -> b -> c.
premise <hc> : and a b.
<hc> c <habc>.

theorem <left conjunction elimination> :
\a b.and a b -> a :=

given a b.
<conjunction elimination> \.
<left>.
 
theorem <right conjunction elimination> :
\a b.and a b -> b :=

given a b.
<conjunction elimination> \.
<right>.

theorem <trivial conjunction elimination> :
\a.and a a -> a :=

given a.
<left conjunction elimination>.

theorem <trivial conjunction introduction> :
\a.a -> and a a :=

given a.
<trivial implication> \.
<conjunction introduction>.

theorem <conjunction symmetric> :
symmetric and :=

given a b.
<conjunction elimination> \.
<reverse conjunction introduction>.

theorem <left non conjunction introduction> :
\a b.not a -> not (and a b) :=

given a b.
<negative converse> \.
<left conjunction elimination>.

theorem <right non conjunction introduction> :
\a b.not b -> not (and a b) :=

given a b.
<negative converse> \.
<right conjunction elimination>.

theorem <disjunction elimination> :
\a b c.(a -> c) -> (b -> c) -> or a b -> c :=

given a b c.
premise <a>.
premise <b>.
premise <d>.
<d> <a> <b>.

theorem <reverse disjunction elimination> :
\a b c.(b -> c) -> (a -> c) -> or a b -> c :=

given a b c.
<implication reverse> \.
<disjunction elimination>.

theorem <non conjunction introduction> :
\a b.
(or (not a) (not b)) ->
not (and a b) :=

given a b.
<disjunction elimination>
  <left non conjunction introduction>
  <right non conjunction introduction>.

theorem <left non conjunction elimination> :
\a b.a -> not (and a b) -> not b :=
 
given a b.
<implication transitive reverse>
  <negative converse> \.
<conjunction introduction>.

theorem <right non conjunction elimination> :
\a b.b -> not (and a b) -> not a :=

given a b.
<implication transitive reverse>
  <negative converse> \.
<reverse conjunction introduction>.

theorem <left disjunction introduction> :
\a b.a -> or a b :=

given a b.
premise <ha>.
given c.
premise <hac>.
<left> \.
<hac> \.
<ha>.

theorem <right disjunction introduction> :
\a b.b -> or a b :=

given a b.
premise <hb>.
given c.
<left> \.
<syllogy> \.
<hb>.

theorem <trivial disjunction introduction> :
\a.a -> or a a :=

given a.
<left disjunction introduction>.

theorem <trivial disjunction elimination> :
\a.or a a -> a :=

given a.
premise <hd>.
<trivial implication> <hd> \.
<implication reflexive>.

theorem <disjunction symmetric> :
symmetric or :=

given a b.
premise <hab>.
given c.
<implication reverse> \.
<hab>.

theorem <left disjunction elimination> :
\a b.not b -> or a b -> a :=

given a b.
<implication transitive>
  <false antecedent> \.
<disjunction elimination>
  <implication reflexive>.

theorem <right disjunction elimination> :
\a b.not a -> or a b -> b :=

given a b.
<implication transitive>
  <false antecedent> \.
<reverse disjunction elimination> 
  <implication reflexive>.

theorem <non disjunction introduction> :
\a b.not a -> not b -> not (or a b) :=

given a b.
<disjunction elimination>.

theorem <non disjunction conjunction> :
\a b.and (not a) (not b) -> not (or a b) :=

given a b.
<conjunction elimination> \.
<disjunction elimination>.

theorem <left non disjunction elimination> :
\a b.not (or a b) -> not b :=

given a b.
<implication transitive> \.
<right disjunction introduction>.

theorem <right non disjunction elimination> :
\a b.not (or a b) -> not a :=

given a b.
<implication transitive> \.
<left disjunction introduction>.

theorem <negative conjunction> :
\a b.not (or a b) -> and (not a) (not b) :=

given a b.
premise <hnd>.
given c.
<binary syllogy> [
  <right non disjunction elimination> <hnd>] [
  <left non disjunction elimination> <hnd>].

theorem <left disjunction false> :
\a.or false a -> a :=

given a.
<disjunction elimination>
  <of false>
  <implication reflexive>.

theorem <right disjunction false> :
\a.or a false -> a :=

given a.
<disjunction elimination>
  <implication reflexive>
  <of false>.

theorem <left biconditional elimination> :
\a b.iff a b -> b -> a :=

given a b.
<right conjunction elimination>.

theorem <right biconditional elimination> :
\a b.iff a b -> a -> b :=

given a b.
<left conjunction elimination>.

theorem <biconditional introduction> :
\a b.(a -> b) -> (b -> a) -> iff a b :=

given a b.
<conjunction introduction>.

theorem <reverse biconditional introduction> :
\a b.(b -> a) -> (a -> b) -> iff a b :=

given a b.
<reverse conjunction introduction>.

theorem <biconditional reflexive> :
reflexive iff :=

given a.
<trivial conjunction introduction> \.
<implication reflexive>.

theorem <biconditional symmetric> :
symmetric iff :=

given a b.
<conjunction symmetric>.

theorem <biconditional transitive> :
transitive iff :=

given a b c.
premise <hab> : iff a b.
premise <hbc> : iff b c.
<hab> (iff a c) \.
premise <iab> : a -> b.
premise <iba> : b -> a.
<hbc> (iff a c) \.
premise <ibc> : b -> c.
premise <icb> : c -> b.
lemma <hac> : a -> c :=
  <implication transitive> a b c <iab> <ibc>.
lemma <hca> : c -> a :=
  <implication transitive> c b a <icb> <iba>.
<biconditional introduction> a c <hac> <hca>.

theorem <universal biconditional> :
\p q.(\x.iff (p x) (q x)) -> iff (\x.p x) (\x.q x) :=

given p q.
premise <f> : \x.iff (p x) (q x).
<biconditional introduction> (\x.p x) (\x.q x) [
  premise <g> : \x.p x.
  given x.
  <right biconditional elimination> (p x) (q x) [<f> x] [<g> x]] [
  premise <g> : \x.q x.
  given x.
  <left biconditional elimination> (p x) (q x) [<f> x] [<g> x]].

theorem <trivial conjunction iff> :
\a.iff (and a a) a :=

given a.
<biconditional introduction>
  (and a a) a [
  <trivial conjunction elimination> a] [
  <trivial conjunction introduction> a].

theorem <trivial disjunction iff> :
\a.iff (or a a) a :=

given a.
<biconditional introduction>
  (or a a) a [
  <trivial disjunction elimination> a] [
  <trivial disjunction introduction> a].

title: 033 Conditional
text:
033 Conditional

define if :=
\c a b.and (iff c a) (iff (not c) b).

theorem <true conditional> :
\a b.if true a b -> a :=

given a b.
premise <hc> : if true a b.
<hc> a \.
premise <ha> : iff true a.
premise <hb> : iff (not true) b.
<right biconditional elimination>
  true a
  <ha> <true>.

theorem <false conditional> :
\a b.if false a b -> b :=

given a b.
premise <hc> : if false a b.
<hc> b \.
premise <ha> : iff false a.
premise <hb> : iff (not false) b.
<right biconditional elimination>
  (not false) b
  <hb> <true>.

title: 034 Existence
text:
034 Existence (* # Existence Existence is defined so that we can find a witness for the predicate. *) define exist := \p c.(\x.p x -> c) -> c. theorem : \x p.p x -> exist p := given x p. premise

. given c. premise . x \.

. theorem : \p c.(\x.p x -> c) -> exist p -> c := given p c. premise . premise . c . theorem : \p.(\x.p x) -> exist p := given p. premise . given c. premise . c \. c. theorem : \p.not (\x.not (p x)) -> irrefutable (exist p) := given p. premise . premise . \. given x. premise . \. x \. . (* We can prove that existence to be irrefutable. Predicates of the propositional logic correspond to sets in naive set theory. In set theory, the axiom of choice is equivalent to the statement that a negations of the complement exists. "not all things are unseen, so there exists something seen." *) define choice := \p.regular (exist p). theorem : \p.choice p -> not (\x.not (p x)) -> exist p := given p. premise . premise . \. \. .

title: 035 Equality
text:
035 Equality

define eq :=
\a b c.c a -> c b.

theorem <equality reflexive> :
reflexive eq :=

given a c.
<implication reflexive>.

theorem <equality symmetric> :
symmetric eq :=

given a b.
<congruent> (\b.eq b a) \.
<equality reflexive>.

theorem <equality transitive> :
transitive eq :=

given a b c.
<congruent> (\b.eq b c -> eq a c) \.
<implication reflexive>.

theorem <equality transitive reverse> :
transitive_reverse eq :=

given a b c.
<implication reverse> \.
<equality transitive>.

theorem <right equality> :
\a b.eq a b -> a -> b :=

given a b.
<special> (eq a b) id.

theorem <left equality> :
\a b.eq a b -> b -> a :=

given a b.
<implication transitive>
  <equality symmetric> \.
<right equality>.

theorem <biconditional of equality> :
\a b.eq a b -> iff a b :=

given a b.
premise <e>.
<biconditional introduction> [
  <right equality> <e>] [
  <left equality> <e>].

title: 037 Congruence
text:
037 Congruence

theorem <congruent argument> :
\c a b.eq a b -> eq (c a) (c b) :=

given c a b.
<congruent> (\b.eq (c a) (c b)) \.
<equality reflexive>.

theorem <congruent function> :
\c a b.eq a b -> eq (a c) (b c) :=

given c a b.
<congruent> (\b.eq (a c) (b c)) \.
<equality reflexive>.

theorem <right substitution> :
\c a b.eq a b -> c a -> c b :=

given c a b.
<implication transitive>
  <congruent argument> \.
<right equality>.

theorem <left substitution> :
\c a b.eq a b -> c b -> c a :=

given c a b.
<implication transitive>
  <congruent argument> \.
<left equality>.

theorem <left equality elimination> :
\c a b.c b -> eq a b -> c a :=

given c a b.
<implication reverse> \.
<left substitution>.

theorem <right equality elimination> :
\c a b.c a -> eq a b -> c b :=

given c a b.
<implication reverse> \.
<right substitution>.

theorem <false ne true> :
neq false true :=

<implication reverse>
  <left equality>
  <true>.

theorem <const ne seq> :
neq const seq :=

<implication transitive> [
  <congruent argument>
    (pair false true)] \.
<false ne true>.

title: 050 Decision
text:
050 Decision

(*

Intuitionistic logic speaks subtly where
classical logic shouts with crass.

In classical logic, the excluded middle property
is usually stated as `or a (not a)`, and
is not distinguished from `not (and a (not a))`.

In this logic, the latter is the excluded
middle property, while the former, called
`decided` has a related but different meaning.

*)

theorem <excluded middle> :
\a.not (and a (not a)) :=

given a.
<conjunction elimination> \.
<irrefutable of>.

(*

`decided`, on the other hand, means that
we have a proof one way or the other.

*)

define decided :=
\x.or x (not x).

theorem <decided of> :
\a.a -> decided a :=

given a.
<left disjunction introduction>.

theorem <decided of not> :
\a.not a -> decided a :=

given a.
<right disjunction introduction>.

theorem <decided negation> :
\a.decided a -> decided (not a) :=

given a.
premise <da>.
<implication reverse>
  <da> <decided of> \.
<implication transitive>
  <irrefutable of> \.
<decided of not>.

theorem <not undecided> :
\a.irrefutable (decided a) :=

given a.
premise <nda>.
<nda> \.
<decided of not> \.
<negative converse>
  <decided of>
  <nda>.

theorem <regular of decided> :
\a.decided a -> regular a :=

given a.
<implication reverse> \.
<left disjunction elimination>.

theorem <not indefinite> :
\a.irrefutable (regular a) :=

given a.
<irrefutable implication> [
  
  <implication reverse> \.
  premise <ia>.
  <disjunction elimination>
    <implication reflexive> \.
    premise <na>.
    <ia> <na> false] [
  
  premise <nda>.
  <nda> \.
  <right disjunction introduction> \.
  <negative converse>
    <decided of> <nda>].

title: 062 Maybe
text:
062 Maybe

define none :=
\a b.a.

define some :=
\x a b.b x.

define maybe' :=
\o p.p none -> (\x.p (some x)) -> p o.

define maybe :=
\a.or (eq a none) (exist \x.eq a (some x)).

define on_some :=
\a f.a none f.

theorem <none maybe> :
\a.maybe none :=

given a.
